# Understanding Cairns: A Summary

## Pulses and Growth

A pulse is how a cairn grows. When you pulse a cairn, it gains height in two ways: first by adding its stride (a fixed property of that cairn), and second by adding an amount equal to the number of complete strides that fit into the current height.

The key insight is that you must count the full strides fresh each time. If you pulse multiple times, you don't reuse the count from before—you look at the new height and count how many strides fit into that updated height.

## Leaks: Proportional Loss

Some cairns have leaks, which remove marks proportionally. After each pulse, you check how many complete leak-sizes fit into the new pulsed height, then subtract that count. The leak applies only to the height after the pulse happens, not before.

## Drains: Consistent Loss

Drains work differently from leaks. In a drained cairn, each cycle applies a pulse and then removes a fixed number of marks. You repeat this cycle until the height falls to zero or below. There's no shortcut—you must trace through each cycle individually because the count of full strides changes as the height evolves.

## Working Backwards: Finding Origins

To find a starting height, you reverse the pulse operation. You know the final height and need to find what height, when pulsed, would produce it. Test candidate heights by pulsing them and checking if they give your target. Repeat backwards through multiple pulses.

## Merging Cairns

When merging two cairns, you use shares (expressed in tenths), a tether (adjustment value), and apply the formula: floor(share₁ × height₁) + floor(share₂ × height₂) + tether. The tether is essential—different tethers give different results even with identical shares.
